title: Part 2 - Giving a talk
subtitle: Notes, keeping going and Fluency and Coherence
summary: Turn the task card into notes, speak for the full two minutes without running dry, and link your ideas so the talk is easy to follow.

lesson.heading: What the task card gives you
lesson.text: The examiner hands you a booklet with a topic and the ideas you must talk about. There are **four instructions** and it is important to address each one. You get about a minute to make notes on extra paper, then you speak for **one to two minutes**.

examples.text: *Describe a time when you helped someone.*
*You should say:* **who you helped and why**
*and explain* **how you felt about helping this person**

lesson.note: You are usually asked to choose a person, place, time or thing and explain why you chose it - then to describe one or two specific examples and give your own feelings or reactions.

lesson.heading: Notes that actually help
lesson.text: Write down the **key words from the task** - they organise your thoughts for you. Do not write too much: you need to be able to glance at your notes and find your next idea instantly.

examples.text: **A list** - *Who and how long? / Why I chose him / How he has influenced my life / My feelings*
examples.note: Each heading is a point on the card, with a few words under it.

examples.text: **A mind map** - the topic in the middle, four branches numbered 1-4.
examples.note: Numbering the branches gives you the order to speak in.

examples.text: Single words beat long phrases; long phrases beat whole sentences.
Organise your ideas **clockwise** on the page rather than in a random order.

lesson.note: As you talk, only glance at your notes briefly. **Do not read directly from them**, and keep eye contact with the examiner.

lesson.heading: If you run out after one minute
lesson.text: It happens to many candidates. There are four things you can do, and all of them are better than stopping.

examples.text: Look at the question again - did you miss any details out?
Refer back to an earlier point in your talk and add more.

lesson.note: These phrases buy you time out loud: *As I said earlier ...*, *At the beginning I mentioned ...*, *I don't think I've said ...*, *Now, what else can I say?*, *I'd just like to add something about ...*, *One thing I forgot to mention ...*

lesson.heading: Fluency and Coherence are two different things

left.label: Coherence
left.text: How easy it is for the listener to follow your ideas.
examples: *You asked me to describe a time when I helped someone. **To that aim**, I've chosen to talk about Aniseto.*
*I went to visit my uncle just as a tourist **but then** I helped him.*
*I'm not very good at English **but** I could help him a little.*
*I could practise my English too, **so** it wasn't just for him, it was also for me.*

right.label: Fluency
right.text: The speed of your delivery and how hesitant you are.
examples: Pausing to find one word is normal; pausing in every sentence is not.
Chunking words together naturally makes you sound more fluent than speaking faster does.

lesson.note: Pronouns connect ideas as well as linking words do - *him*, *he*, *this*, *that* all point back to something you already said.

lesson.heading: Signalling where you are in the talk
rows: I've decided to talk about ... / To that aim, I've chosen ...
I think s/he has influenced my life by ...
When I think of him/her, I feel ...

lesson.text: Part 2 ends with a short rounding-off question. Answer it fully - it is still part of the assessed test, not small talk on the way out.

exercises.prompt: How long do you speak for in Part 2, and how long do you get to prepare?
options: 1-2 minutes, after about a minute of notes
3-4 minutes, after two minutes of notes
As long as you like, until the examiner stops you
exercises.explanation: The examiner gives you paper and about a minute, then you talk for one to two minutes and are told when to stop.

exercises.prompt: Sort these approaches to making notes.

items.text: using the key words from the task card as headings
organising ideas clockwise on the page
numbering the branches of a mind map
scattering the notes randomly on the page
writing so much that you have to read from the page

exercises.prompt: You have run out of ideas after one minute. Complete the phrase that buys you time: *___ I said earlier, my uncle doesn't speak English.*
exercises.explanation: *As I said earlier* refers back to a point you have already made and lets you add to it - one of the four ways to keep going.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase with the point in the talk where it belongs.

pairs.left: When I think of her, I feel ...

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between Fluency and Coherence?
options: They are the same criterion under two names
Fluency is speed and hesitancy; Coherence is how easily the listener follows your ideas
Fluency is vocabulary; Coherence is grammar
Fluency is Part 1 only; Coherence is Part 2 only
exercises.explanation: A candidate can be fluent but incoherent - fast, but jumping between unconnected ideas.

exercises.statement: You should read your talk directly from the notes you made.
exercises.explanation: Glance at them briefly. Reading aloud destroys your fluency score and breaks eye contact with the examiner.

exercises.prompt: Build an opening sentence that refers back to the task card.
exercises.answer: You asked me to describe a time when I helped someone.
exercises.explanation: Melanie opens this way, then follows with *To that aim, I've chosen to talk about Aniseto* - clear signposting from the first line.

exercises.prompt: A task card reads *Describe a time when you helped someone.* Which of these must your talk cover?

items.text: how you felt about helping them
whether you would do it again

exercises.prompt: *I went to visit my uncle just as a tourist, ___ then I helped him.* Which word marks the change of direction?
exercises.explanation: Small connectors like *but*, *so*, *also* and *because* are what a good Coherence score is actually made of.

exercises.statement: The short rounding-off question at the end of Part 2 is part of the assessed test.
exercises.explanation: It is not small talk on the way out - answer it as fully as you answered the talk itself.
